utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone after a relatively long time not having been in court. Mr. Krajisnik, I haven't seen you for a couple of weeks now. So before we start, may I ask you, Madam Registrar, to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The next witness the Prosecution intends to call is a protected witness, and it will be you, Mr. Gaynor, who will examine the witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps, just for the record, it's Mr. Hannis and Mr. Gaynor who appear as counsel for the Prosecution. It's Ms. Loukas and Mr. Stewart and Ms. Cmeric who appear for the Defence. And I've forgotten to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We're assisted by Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had forgotten that. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. If there is nothing which would need urgent attention, I would like to invite the Prosecution to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are two tiny points, one which is only -- I do realise that I was in a position of taking issue with Your Honour's very first sentence this morning because, of course, what Your Honour describes as a relatively long time we describe as a relatively short time, but we'll leave that issue. The only other point -- the reason -- I wouldn't have got to my feet for that, Your Honour, but simply to say that I think Your Honour said, and it was a slip of the tongue, that Mr. Krajisnik was represented this morning by me and Ms. Cmeric. I think that's what Your Honour said, if I heard correctly. Of course, I'm with Ms. Loukas as my co-counsel, but we may have misheard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I first mentioned your names. As a matter of fact, I took the -- perhaps the wrong order by first mentioning, I think, Ms. Loukas, who is not lead counsel, but you, without any doubt, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know whether that happened. That would not be an issue for us, Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Assisted by Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have taken time. I misheard. It's Ms. Loukas, myself and Ms. Cmeric, in that order of something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the next witness into the courtroom. The next witness is protected by face distortion, by pseudonym, which will be 044.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, I'd just like to give Your Honour an indication as to how we intend to proceed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This witness is from the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Specifically he's from the Japra Valley. Now, another witness testified in relation to events in the Japra Valley on the 22nd of April. The testimony of this witness is cumulative in part to the testimony of Mr. Alic who testified on the 22nd of April. In particular, it's cumulative in respect to the transport of Muslim civilians on cattle cars out of the Japra Valley and in respect of detention of Muslim civilian males and the Mlakve stadium in Bosanski Novi. In respect of those matters, we do not intend to examine the witness to any great extent. We might touch on a few details here and there, and we will be submitting his statement pursuant to Rule 89(F). Now, I won't be seeking admission of his statement until the end of his testimony when he's had a chance to clarify and amplify certain aspects in his statement. I trust that meets your approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We usually give a final decision on admission of all evidence, as a matter of fact, at the very end of the testimony of a witness, but it's good to know that you intend to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. 044, as I will call you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- since certain protective measures are effective in respect of you. That means that no one can see your face, your face is distorted, and we will not use your name but we'll call you 044. Mr. 044, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. 044.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would request the witness be shown the pseudonym sheet which sets out his name and his date of birth. I'd also request that an exhibit number be assigned to that sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you confirm that that is your name and that that is your date of birth by simply saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could I remind you not to refer to yourself by your name at any point during your testimony nor to any members of your family.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd request that we go into private session very briefly to describe the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before doing so I would like to give the opportunity to Madam Registrar to mention the number attributed to the name sheet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number for the pseudonym sheet is P93, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll then turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now in open session now again. Please proceed, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request that the next exhibit be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the screen in front of you, you see a map of the municipality of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, is Exhibit P78, which you have seen during the testimony of Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, do you see -- just wait for a moment while the image reaches you. Sir, on that map do you see marked in green the village of Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you answer with a yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is the ethnic composition of the village of Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: They're mostly Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How many Muslims were in Suhaca before conflict broke out in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: About 2.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I request that the next exhibit be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, this next exhibit is a map --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll explain to Your Honours what the next map is. This is a map showing the ethnic breakdown of Bosnia following the 1991 census. Your Honours will see, in the bottom left-hand corner is a legend. It's clear from that legend that blue means an area with a Serb majority, green means an area with a Muslim majority. This is exhibit is P68, tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at the area around the Bosanski Novi municipality, which will be selected for you now. Do you see the area in green around Bosanski Novi, sir?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell me, what does that area in green approximate to?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Well, it represents the area where the majority were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm referring to the area in green.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Uh-huh. The green area was the Japra Valley, and the villages in the Japra Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 11th of December, 1998?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And over the past few days have you had an opportunity to review your statement in detail?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd just like you to close your statement for the moment, and we're going to correct and clarify a number of matters raised in your statement. There is no need for you to consult it. I'll direct you to the relevant -- I'll direct Their Honours to the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I will be referring to certain paragraphs in the statement, Your Honours, if you wish to follow while I'm referring to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraph 8 of your statement, you're talking about the dismissal of non-Serbs from employment in Bosanski Novi. You say that you knew of three men who were dismissed: Mr. Adem Barjaktarevic, who worked for the municipality; Mr. Husein Ekic, who was a driver for the municipality; and a man called Hamdija, who was a policeman. What is the ethnicity of those three people?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Those three people were Muslims, and it is true that they were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were any Serbs, to your knowledge, dismissed?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement - paragraph 12, Your Honours - you referred to a day in March 1992 when you went to the Serb village of Josava and you and other villagers from Suhaca waited there for five hours while Suhaca was searched. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Who searched your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Mostly soldiers, Serb soldiers, and they took away two men, two Muslim men, to protect them, to ensure that houses were not mined, but mostly it was Serb soldiers who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What were they looking for?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: They were looking for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Later in your statement - paragraph 14, Your Honours - you say that you saw a helicopter land and you saw two cars near that spot. Where did that helicopter land?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I did see a helicopter, and it handed in the hamlet of Halilovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How far away from you was the helicopter at the time that it landed?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: About one kilometre as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you actually see the helicopter touch down on the ground?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw it land, and we moved in the direction to see what was going on. Two cars went by, and the helicopter took off at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say the cars went by, was that before or after the helicopter took off?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: After the helicopter had landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Were the cars carrying anything?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were carrying weapons. You could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Mostly rifles, Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How many rifles? Five or ten?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: More than that. In the Warburg station wagon car you could see that the boot was full, and in the Lada car they were on the back seat, covered with a blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, who was driving those two cars?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Warburg was driven by Mijo Majkic, who was the son of Niko Majkic from Josava; and the Lada car was driven by Dragan Podunavac, son of Rade. Or the other way around, I'm not sure who was Simo and who was Rade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of those two men?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify the duration of the shelling of Suhaca. This is paragraph 17, Your Honours. How long did the shelling of Suhaca last for?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: A week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, you might want to know that's a correction to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When the shelling first began, was it accurately pinpointing certain buildings?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, they weren't pinpointing accurately. The first day that the shelling took place the shells fell all over, all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it right that after a day or two soldiers in a JNA vehicle visited your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How accurate was the shelling after that visit?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: After that visit, the shelling was more accurate, and they hit part of the old bridge and a garage and a house next to the mosque. About 20 metres away from the mosque, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did they manage to hit the mosque at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, they did not manage to hit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a tendentious question. To phrase a question "Did they manage to hit the mosque" contains an implication which should not be there in the question. The first question should be whether they hit the mosque. The implication of "manages" is quite clear and is inappropriate in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, it at least suggests that someone was aiming at the mosque, whereas the first question is, I think, what actually happened, unless you ask other questions to the witness, but then of course you should first of all find out whether the witness has any knowledge, specific knowledge, of those firing shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I withdraw the question. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask you also to -- you ask a question about paragraph 16 and the five weeks were amended, and one week. What about the sixth week? Could you clarify that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, is it still the sixth week or is it the first week after the shelling, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At the end of the shelling --

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the first week.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: That is to say, those six weeks was the entire period from the shelling to the arrival in the village of Blagaj, and when the weapons were handed over, the shelling and the arrival in Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How soon after the end of the shelling were you instructed to leave your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Two days after the shelling they came again with Pinzgauer, a military vehicle, and they said we had to leave because they said they were no longer able to protect us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say "they came again in a Pinzgauer," who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The soldiers, the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could look at your screen, at the image on that screen. Do you recognise that building, sir?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes. It's the mosque in Suhaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at the structural damage on the building itself, do you have any idea how that was caused?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes. This was caused by the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At this point I'd ask that the photograph be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you said that the damage was caused by an explosion. I'll pause just for a moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P94.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said that the damage was caused by an explosion. Do you know who caused that explosion?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I didn't see, but it was done by the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was this explosion caused during the shelling of your village or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The explosion took place after the shelling. While we were still in Blagaj, we heard the explosion, the detonations, and a day after that two men came back to the village of Suhaca to pick up a man who was killed. And when they returned, they told us that both the mosques had been destroyed and that that was the explosion that we had heard the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 17, Your Honours. Sir, when you left your village, prior to your leaving the village, what state were the houses in?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: A normal state. They were all standing, intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see any fires in any part of your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: That day when we were expelled to Blagaj, the houses were on fire, the surrounding houses on the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the cause of that fire?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The cause of the fire was that the people, the soldiers, had set fire to them, the ones I had seen with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say "the soldiers," could you specify which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: They were the Serb soldiers. They shot, creating fear amongst us, and we saw them enter the houses. They were the houses in the -- on the surrounding hills that were abandoned. They left the houses, and ten minutes later the houses were burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you and the rest of the inhabitants left your village, did you all leave your village or did some of you remain behind, some of the Muslim population of Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: All of us left at once. Just an old woman stayed on, and the Serb soldiers drove her in later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to refer you to paragraph 24 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, you spent 17 days in Blagaj Japra, and at the end of those 17 days you saw military vehicles, buses, and a Serb media vehicle pass through the village. What -- when you say "military vehicles," what kind of military vehicles do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: A military bus carrying soldiers passed through, a tank, a civilian truck, and a Golf car belonging to the Belgrade TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Focusing on the tank for a moment, did the tank stop?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The tank passed through the village and came to a halt in the hamlet of Troske, 2 to 300 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you recall the direction in which the tank's turret was facing?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: When it stopped in Troske, it turned in the direction of Blagaj Japra and at that moment soldiers started getting off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in Blagaj Japra is it right that there was a very large group of Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. All Muslims from the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to refer you to page 7, paragraph 51 and 52 and 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to bring you forward to the end of your detention period at the Mlakve stadium in Bosanski Novi. Now, the day before the last day of your detention, you signed a document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was that document?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: One day before my last day came to leave the camp, soldiers came together with two civilians from the municipality. They brought us a document which read, "I - and then the name and the surname - renounce all my movable and immovable property to the Republika Srpska and the municipality of Bosanski Novi of my own free will." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Where did you sign that document? Where were you standing or sitting physically at that time?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: We signed that document at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you sign that document voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, I did not sign it voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did anyone, to the best of your knowledge, sign it voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: As far as I know, out of those 700 people at the stadium, no one signed it voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did anyone resist in any way the signing of that document?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, one man resisted, but he was a sick man, and at the end, his brother signed for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just focusing on that incident: What happened to the man when he refused to sign the document?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: When he refused to sign the document, a soldier hit him with a pistol on the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Refer Your Honours to paragraph 53. Sir, you stayed that in the stadium a person called Zoran called out 18 names. Who was Zoran?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I'm not sure who Zoran is, but I think that before the war he had lived in Dobrljin, and he was an infamous mobster belonging to the Suha Rebra group.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you -- Zoran called out 18 names, you said. Could you tell the Court the occupations of the people whose names were called out?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: That is correct. He called out Resad and Dzafer, who were presidents of the Bosanski Novi SDA. Then Muslimovic, who had a private business; he produced plastic bags. Then they called out Salco. I only know his nickname. He was not a local. He was not from the area. He was a teacher who had come to work there. Then Nedjo, who had a business, a trucking business. And then they called out Hasan Kantarevic, Hadjo, who also had a small trucking business. And Fuad Adilovic, who was just another a worker, employee. I don't know why they had called out his name. Others were also ordinary people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Of the men whose names were called out, what happened to those men?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: After the signing of the document and after these people had been called out, they tied their hands and they took them away in the direction of Bosanski Novi town, on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see those men again?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Only two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, have you had an opportunity to review not only your statement but also the very last page of the document on your desk, which you can now consult. And just concentrating on that page, is that a set of corrections signed by you on the 1st of June, 2001?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that statement incorporating those corrections and incorporating the clarifications which you provided today true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is there anything you wish to add to that statement or amend in any way?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, nothing in particular, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd ask that the witness be shown the next exhibit, and I'd request that the next exhibit be given a number. While that document is being circulated, I'm just going to summarise briefly what it is. This is a document prepared by the cantonal court in Bihac. It's a record of an exhumation conducted on the 20th October 1998. The exhumation was attended by, among others, an anthropologist, Elvira Kovolovski [phoen] from Iceland, representatives of Physicians for Human Rights, representatives of the office of the High Representative, representatives of the International Police Task Force, and representatives of SFOR. At the bottom of page 2 of the English language version of that document, statement, the document indicates that on the 13th of October, 1998, a mass grave was exhumed at the Blagaj-Japra-Dubrava location. Now, I'd like to concentrate on page 3 of the English language translation of this document, and I would like to draw the witness's attention to the B/C/S original just headed with the number 00878525. It says in this document that ten skeletonised bodies were found and marked by numbers 1 to 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to concentrate on the paragraph beginning with "During the autopsy..." That's the fourth paragraph on the version you're looking at. Sir, I'd like you to tell the Court if you recognise any of the names set down in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you read out for the Court the names which you recognise.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Sulejman Burzic from Blagaj Japra. Nijaz Isakovic, Hasan Merzihic. I don't see any other names, but I know that there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw Sulejman Burzic?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I saw Sulejman Burzic for the last time in the compound of the Japra company.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was he doing the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Well, he was in the compound of the company, like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The man was killed by a Serb soldier by the name of Dragan who had come from the direction of Svodna. Later I heard that he worked in Svodna, that he was in charge of issuing birth certificates, that he worked at the registrar's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say the man was killed, did you see him being killed?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was killed some five to ten metres from where I stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said you recognised the name Nijaz Isakovic. When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes. I recognised his name. Nijaz Isakovic and his brother Karanfil were standing on the bridge with their hands tied at the moment we were crossing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Why -- who had tied their hands?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I did not see that. By the time I reached the bridge, they had already been tied up. But it was there that we were checked by the Serb soldiers, and I believe it was the Serb soldiers who had tied them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You mentioned that the last time you saw this man he was with his brother Karanfil. Now, on the paragraph in front of you, you might see in about third last line the last name Karanfil Isakovic, born on the 7th of April, 1968, do you believe that to be the same man?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You said you recognised the name Hasan Merzihic. When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Hasan Merzihic worked as a waiter in Suhaca. He was with us in Blagaj in the compound of Japra.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: After we had been put into the cattle cars, a soldier, a Serb soldier arrived whom I didn't know, neither by name nor by sight. He called out three names amongst whom was Hasan Merzihic. Hasan Merzihic spoke up and the soldier took him out of the wagon and took him in the direction of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: He was shot at in the chest and then again two times in the head by this soldier, some 20 to 30 metres away from the wagon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify with the registrar whether that document has been given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is P95, and the English translation P95.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd request that the witness be shown the next exhibit, and I'd request the next exhibit be given an exhibit number. I'll just describe it briefly for Your Honours. The next exhibit is a document prepared by the public security station in Bosanski Novi under the security services centre of Banja Luka of the Ministry of the Interior, Srpska Republika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Gaynor, may I just ask you for one clarification. The English version, that is P95.1, starts a handwritten 9.480. If I look, however, at the B/C/S original, I do see no handwriting at all. So I wonder whether the translation has been made from this very document or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, as Your Honour would probably appreciate, it's very possible that the translation has been made of a separate copy of this document. I hadn't noticed the discrepancy myself. We can try and get hold of the version of this document which contains 9.480 in the top right-hand corner, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's always good if the translation mentions something that we find that in the original as well. So if you could find the corresponding original, that would be certainly an improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next exhibit, I was hoping it -- could it be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P96, and the English version P96.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As I was explaining, Your Honour, this is a report which, according to the last page of the document, was declared on the 15th of August, 1992 in Bosanski Novi, signed by Dragomir Kutiljevac. And the opening paragraph suggests that the report was prepared on the basis of the decision by the chief of the Banja Luka CSB of 14th August, 1992, to establish a commission to inspect the municipalities and public security stations of Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Sanski Most. The second page, at the very top, this document records that the forces of the Bosanski Novi Territorial Defence Municipal Staff and the military police began to round up non-Serb citizens at the Mlakve stadium without the knowledge of or consultations with the Bosanski Novi public security station. Now, we're not going to concentrate on which organs of the RS government knew what at this stage, Your Honour. I would simply direct the witness, sir, to the last paragraph on page 2 of the B/C/S. That's the second paragraph on page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to read out a few phrases bit by bit and then ask you for your comments. This is referring to the detention of Bosnian Muslims at the Mlakve stadium. The first sentence says: "According to our information, the persons at the collection centre were occasionally permitted visits by their families." How many visits by your family did you receive while you were at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I did not have any visits at all. It was during the last two days, at the time when UNPROFOR was supposed to arrive, that they allowed visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did any of the other detainees receive visits from their families?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Families did arrive. My family paid me a visit as well, but they were not allowed entry into the premises. They would be standing there for hours on end and then, afterwards, they would just -- they would just go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The second sentence of the document in front of you reads: "The municipal Territorial Defence staff regularly provided them with food, which meant one cooked meal a day." Sir, could you tell us how much food you received during your six-week detention at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: We received food once a week, and usually they would distribute one loaf of bread amongst 12 people, and they brought water - actually tea - in metal containers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Was the food sufficient?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, the food was not sufficient. There was very little food, and there were very little dishes. Also, we had about 12 plates and spoons, so you had to wait for others to finish so that you can use their dishes and spoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How much did you weigh on your arrival at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I weighed 86 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How much did you weigh at the end of your detention at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: At the end of my detention, after I arrived in Croatia, I weighed 75 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How long were you in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Forty-six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next sentence of the document in front of you reads: "The citizens at the collection centre had at their disposal the use of the football field and the premises of the football club as sleeping quarters." Sir, did you use the football field for recreational purposes?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No. We could use the football field, only half of it, to the left and to the right of the goal posts. We were not allowed to move further. As for the premises of the football club, we did use them as sleeping quarters. I slept in one of the changing rooms, together with 21 other detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you have a mattress, blankets, pillow?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, we didn't have anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How often did you change your clothes during those six weeks in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I never changed my clothes. I didn't have anything to change into. I had a pair of trousers on, a T-shirt, and I was barefoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next line of the document in front of you reads: "If necessary, they were given medical care." What medical care did you receive while you were at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I didn't receive any medical care, nor did anyone else, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to page 5 in the B/C/S version. Also page 5 in the English version. A little halfway down this page it says here that: "Proceeding from a decision on the voluntary moving out of citizens issued by the government of the AR Krajina and an order by the Bosanski Novi municipality Crisis Staff on criteria for voluntary moving out, the Bosanski Novi public security station has, in accordance with due procedure, dealt with citizens' requests in the following manner." Under that, it says: "Permanently counciled residency 5.680 persons." A little further down the page, it says, according to ethnicity, the total number of counciled residencies was Muslims, 5.629. Paragraph below, this document says, and I'll just read the relevant part: "Citizens who have moved out voluntarily have given written statements to the competent municipal organ that their moving was voluntary." Sir, there are several references there to the voluntary moving of Muslim civilians. Did you voluntarily decide to leave your village of Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: That is not correct. I did not leave the area voluntarily nor was that the case with my fellow villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know any Muslim from the Japra Valley who voluntarily decided to leave?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, I do not. There were no such Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you voluntarily surrender your property to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was forced to do that at the stadium. I was forced to signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you know anybody, any Muslim who voluntarily surrendered his or her property to the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order that the public may be fully informed about the written evidence of this witness, we have prepared a written summary which I'm willing to read out now or after the witness has left, as you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's usually done in the presence of the witness because, finally, it is a summary of his own statement. I take it that the summary has been provided to the Defence prior to this hearing so that they could check whether the summary was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, I received it with my breakfast this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's prior, but not a long time prior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is technically prior, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I assume that in the future such summaries will be provided at an earlier stage than at breakfast for the Defence, especially when we have morning sessions. Mr. Stewart, were you able to review the summary to the extent that you can pronounce on whether you would agree this to be a proper summary of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was all part of the normal working day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It means early breakfast, doesn't it. Mr. Gaynor, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This witness is from the Muslim village of Suhaca in the Japra River valley in the municipality of Bosanski Novi, north-west Bosnia-Herzegovina. The witness's evidence focuses on the expulsion of the Muslim population of the Japra Valley in 1992 and the witness's subsequent detention in the Mlakve football stadium in Bosanski Novi town. Suhaca contains no military facilities of any kind. President of the SDA Suhaca village was Sifet Barjaktarevic. Mr. Barjaktarevic was also the representative for Suhaca in the Bosanski Novi Municipal Assembly. President of the SDS in the nearby Serb village of Josava was Ranko Balaban. Before the outbreak of war, the witness saw a military helicopter land at the nearby hamlet. Near the helicopter he saw two vehicles which subsequently drove off to Josava. In March 1992, Serbs in Josava established a Crisis Staff. At the end of March, Sifet Barjaktarevic began a series of meetings with Ranko Balaban in Josava. As a result of those meetings, the Suhaca Muslims surrendered their weapons, which were mainly hunting rifles. After the weapons were surrendered the Muslim inhabitants of Suhaca were instructed to assemble in a field at Josava village. While the population of Suhaca were thus assembled at Josava, Serbs searched Suhaca for more weapons. The Suhaca Muslims then returned home. A week after the disarmament of the Muslims of Suhaca, the shelling of Suhaca began without warning. Shelling lasted throughout the day. Due to a barricade, it was impossible to leave the village during the shelling. The shelling appeared to be coming from the Serb villages of Josava and Rasula. After it ended, Serb soldiers in a JNA vehicle arrived in Suhaca and told the villagers they would have to leave their village. By this time panic had taken hold in the Muslim population of the Japra Valley. A convoy of approximately 8.000 people from the villages of Gornji Agici, Dedici, Donji Agici, Hozici and Suhaca left their villages and headed towards the town of Bosanski Novi. The convey got as far as Blagaj, where it was stopped at the bridge by Serb military police. There, two of the Serb military policemen took two brothers, bound their hands, and detained them. The witness has not seen the two brothers since that day. At the bridge in Blagaj, the Muslims were ordered to leave their cars and tractors, to cross the bridge and to get on a train that was waiting for them. The Muslims refused. A meeting was held. Sifet Barjaktarevic and other Muslim representatives met Serb representatives, who included JNA captain Bogdan Grab. It was resolved that the Muslims could stay in the village of Blagaj. They slept wherever they could find shelter. Sifet Barjaktarevic went to Bosanski Novi to negotiate with the SDS there. Negotiations with the SDS lasted 17 days. Barjaktarevic went back and forth from Blagaj to Bosanski Novi but no agreement could be reached. In the meantime, the village of Blagaj was shelled by Serbs and JNA soldiers then surrounded Blagaj. At the bridge in Blagaj, Serb military police stripped the assembled Muslims of their jewellery, valuables, and other property. The witness saw three people murdered at the bridge. A Serb soldier called Milan Balaban from Josava selected three civilians and shot them in the chest. In one incident a man was holding a child in his arms before he was killed. Milan Balaban took the child from the man's arms and handed it to its mother and then shot the man 20 metres away from his wife. A soldier with a red beret, called Zoran, ordered that the men be separated from the women and children. The Muslims formed two lines in accordance with these orders and then approached the bridge where they were searched by Serb soldiers and police. Zoran occasionally shot in the air and hit people as they passed. The large group of Muslims was taken to the Japra enterprise compound in Japra village where they were detained. At that location, a man called Dragan who, the witness was told, was the president of the SDS in the village of Svodna, killed a detainee with an AK47 in the view of around a thousand people. JNA captain Bogdan Grab called out the names of specific men on a loudspeaker. Two men responded and were driven away. The soldier with the red beret, called Zoran, called out the name of a detainee and then shot him with six bullets. He then took Sifet Barjaktarevic, the SDA president from Suhaca village, to an embankment, pushed Mr. Barjaktarevic down the embankment, pulled a rifle to his shoulder and fired down the embankment. The witness did not see Mr. Barjaktarevic return. The witness and other Muslims were loaded onto a train of cattle wagons which set off to Doboj, passing through Prijedor and Banja Luka. It stopped at the village of Ostruzna where the Muslims were separated into two groups. Men aged 15 to 60 were locked in rail cars. Women, children, and the elderly were taken in other rail cars to Doboj. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. engine then returned and took four to five cattle wagons, containing over 700 men, towards Bosanski Novi. The train spent the night at Banja Luka. While the witness was on the train, he saw destroyed mosques in the villages of Urije and Prekosanje. On arrival in Bosanski Novi, the men were forced to run through two lines of soldiers and into the Mlakve football stadium. The men were detained in the stadium for about six weeks. They received food once a day and rations were grossly inadequate. Water supplies were also inadequate. Detainees attempted to communicate with UNPROFOR vehicles located on the other side of the River Una in Croatia. They wrote SOS on their coats. One day, an UNPROFOR vehicle acknowledged their signals by flashing its lights. Military police and soldiers guarded the detainees in the stadium. Among the guards was Ranko Balaban, the head of the SDS in Josava village. On the penultimate day of his detention at Mlakve stadium, Serb soldiers forced the witness and other detainees to sign a form. The form stated in effect that the person signing renounced all his movable and immovable property and transferred it to the Republika Srpska. During the signing process in the stadium, soldiers called out the names of SDA members and successful businessmen and led them away. The witness knew ten of those led away. He has not seen or heard of most of those men again. The witness and other Muslims were transported then in a convoy of buses and trucks towards the Croatian border. On the way, the witness saw a number of destroyed mosques. The Orthodox church was intact. At the Croatian border, the Muslims were met by UNPROFOR troops who fed the Muslims and brought them to Karlovac, where the witness was reunited with his wife. The witness's written and oral evidence today is relevant to all counts in the indictment and is relevant in particular to event 3.1 in Schedule A to the indictment, detention facilities 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.5 and 5.6 in Schedule C, and to mosques 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.6, 3.8, 3.9, 3.10, 3.11 in Schedule D of the indictment. Your Honours, it has just come to my realisation that the -- I've not specifically asked the witness regarding whether he saw with his own eyes the mosques numbered in the final two -- the final sentence of that page. If the Defence wishes me to establish those facts I can do so, however if they wish to save time, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we always wish to save time, but on the other hand, we also do wish facts to be established once in awhile, so it would not waste time if I simply say yes, please, would those facts be established in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Gaynor, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that's good advice from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- I will do so. I'll just get a copy of the detention facilities in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you about certain mosques which you might have seen, and I want you to tell us what state you saw those mosques in. And I want you to concentrate on the year 1992 before you left Bosanski Novi. I'll read out the name of the mosque. Please tell us what condition it was in. The first one is Gradska Dzamija in Bosanski Novi town. What state was that mosque in?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: It was in a very good state. It was standing intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see any damage of any kind to that mosque?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: At the exit to Bosanski Novi, it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When -- when was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: It was that last day when they rounded us up from the camps in the buses and trucks. We passed by the mosque in crossing into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say it was destroyed, was it completely razed to the ground or was it merely partially destroyed?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The Vidorije Dzamija was destroyed and the Gradska Dzamija was razed. There was just a grass patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What was the state of the mosque in Urije when you saw it before you left the municipality?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: All the mosques were standing, Urije and Prekosanje were destroyed when we passed by in the train from the Prijedor-Banja Luka direction going to Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'll move on to the mosque in Blagaj Japra. What state was that mosque in when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: In Blagaj Japra, when we arrived the mosque had been hit. The minaret had been hit but it wasn't destroyed. Just a section of it had been toppled. But later on in the Blagaj area, the mosque, it was destroyed because the minaret was made of wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you see with your own eyes evidence of the destruction of that mosque?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes. The mosque in Blagaj Rijeka, I saw that with my own eyes, but they set fire to the surrounding houses, so that's how the mosque came to be on fire too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say "they set fire," who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers. I saw that with my own eyes. They were walking with the civilian government members in the direction --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, the witness seems to have switched to a different mosque, unless I'm simply getting confused by the transcript. It looks as if he has switched to a different mosque, and it may be that Mr. Gaynor will want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, could you concentrate on the mosque in Blagaj Japra. Did you see that mosque with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No. In Blagaj Japra, the mosque had already been hit when we arrived, but I'm talking about Blagaj Rijeka, which was just 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll come to Blagaj Rijeka in a minute, sir. Did you see the Vidorije mosque?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What state was it in?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The roof had been destroyed and the minaret as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, the Blagaj Rijeka mosque, what state was that in?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: While we were in Blagaj Japra, it was standing in a normal state, but afterwards, soldiers turned up, as I had just begun telling you, Serb soldiers turned up with a civilian car, a Lada vehicle, and on the road from Bosanski Novi to Prijedor, that's the road they took, and they would move ten metres ahead, open the boot, shoot or use a hand grenade, and move on. And that's how they set fire to the houses in Blagaj Rijeka and the mosque as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What state was the Stara Suhaca mosque in when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Both mosques were standing intact the day we set out in the direction of Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When you say both mosques, do you mean Stara Suhaca and the Suhaca mosque, the main Suhaca mosque?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony you saw a picture of the Suhaca mosque. Just to clarify, did you see that mosque bearing evidence of destruction with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No. When we set out in the direction of Blagaj, the mosque was standing intact, but that night in Blagaj we heard strong explosions, detonations, and then the next day two men went there to pick up the dead. And when they returned, they told us that both mosques had been destroyed and the mosque which was in the -- the main mosque, in fact, was destroyed so that they weren't able to pass by in the car. They had to go by on foot to pick up the dead man, bring him to the mosque and take him back to Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Subject to one thing. Normally the lectern is made available on this side of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a quick physical task but it does help a lot to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it certainly adds to the equality of arms, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, there is that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the lectern is being transferred, may I just confirm that I formally sought the admission of the statement of this witness pursuant to Rule 89.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I request that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness statement is Exhibit number P97, under seal; and the B/C/S translation P97.1, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that includes the corrections made on the 1st of June which are in this same bundle, as far as I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: -- it should be treated as one bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Treated as one bundle. Now, Mr. Stewart, please proceed. You will now be examined by counsel for the Defence, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, could I just start there at one slightly puzzling point in your evidence which is that you described how you were able to identify arms in cars which went past, and you referred to a Lada car containing weapons which were covered by a blanket on the back seat. I wonder if you could just make it clear how it was that you were able to identify what it was that was covered by a blanket.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Precisely because it wasn't sufficiently covered. The blanket had just been loosely placed over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we go to your statement. You say that -- and this is paragraph 10. The paragraph numbering is the same in your version and in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honour, I'd assumed the witness had a copy of his statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He now has, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you look at paragraph 10, the English version says: "Most of the trouble in our village started when the war in Slovenia was over but when it was at its worst in Croatia." So we're talking about sometime in 1991, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When would you date the start of the trouble in your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Precisely when the war in Slovenia began and spread to Croatia, because all the Serb inhabitants from the surrounding villages went to the war and came back with weapons, ammunition, started shooting, provoking, came in drunken, and although movement wasn't completely restricted, that's when it started. That is to say, you could move around when you had -- absolutely had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Put a month on it, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Well, there's no exact month. It was throughout the time of the war in Slovenia and Croatia, and as time passed, it -- the situation deteriorated until it reached us in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was -- was there any activity by Muslims in your area which contributed to trouble?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: None whatever?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Absolutely none, just small fights which were sort of normal even before the war; brawls.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any -- in your village or in the surrounding area, were there any groups, however large or small, of Muslim extremists?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So do you say that such trouble as there was was entirely one-sided, entirely created or provoked by non-Muslims?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In -- just go back a couple of paragraphs in your statement. First of all, paragraph -- well, more than a couple. Paragraph 4, you referred to a number of officials, officers of the SDA. You referred to Sifet Barjaktarevic and Sefer Kapetanovic and others. Would those people that you mentioned in that paragraph, they were all personally known to you, were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, they were known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 8 of your statement, you say: "Just after the elections," and we're talking about -- or you're talking about the November 1990 elections there, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was still peaceful, you said. The Serbs fired people, and you know of three men who were fired from their jobs. Did you know those men personally?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I knew those three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was Mr. Barjaktarevic's job working for the municipality?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what he did exactly, but he worked in the municipality of Bosanski Novi, in the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what he did?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It followed then that you had no idea of the circumstances in which he lost his job.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: He lost his job just for being a Muslim. I know the man from Suhaca, and he told me himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So he told you himself that he lost his job but you still have no idea what that job was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No. He worked in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. What he did exactly I don't know but after the elections he no longer worked there and I asked why and he said, "Because I'm a Muslim," but he didn't comment. He didn't elaborate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think I asked you whether you had any idea at all -- but if I didn't I'm asking you now -- whether you had any idea at all what his work was for the municipality.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: He certainly wasn't builder in the municipality, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 12 of your statement. You referred to end of March 1992, meeting set up between the Serbs and the SDA, and you refer to a specific meeting, and you say: "As a result of this meeting, the Muslims surrendered their weapons. They were mostly hunting rifles." If they were "mostly" hunting rifles, what were the rest of the weapons that were not hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: They were pistols and two semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you say, "We turned them over in a tractor trailer," are you saying that you were personally involved in the physical handing over of weapons in a tractor trailer?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So precisely, as best as you can do, precisely what, first of all, was the quantity of hunting rifles turned over and what was the quantity of other weapons turned over?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but there were 70 to 80 hunting rifles and some handmade rifles. The rest were pistols and those semi-automatic ones that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What sort of quantify? You gave a number to the hunting rifles, can you give a similar estimate to the number of other weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, I can't give you an exact number, but altogether there would have been about 300 barrels. I wasn't there when the list was compiled, I just did the physical work, loading and unloading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you talk about -- your evidence in your statement is that the Serbs took two of your people and they went back to your village to search the houses for more weapons. The two people that the Serbs took, that didn't include you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: That's right. I stayed in the field with the other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say who those two people were?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: From the village of Suhaca, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Who were they? Did you know them?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I did know them. They were Husein from Suhaca, I think his surname -- I don't need to say his surname, do I? And the other one was Ismet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the search lasted from 11.00 to 4.00 p.m. Do you know if anything was found?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The search went on to late afternoon, but nothing was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I do know that, yes, because those two soldiers came back with the two men, and they said, "Everything's all right. They didn't find anything. You can go home safely," and the soldiers left us and we went back to our own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if that would be a suitable moment for the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is a suitable moment for you, Mr. Stewart, we'll have a break now. We will have a break until five minutes to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you -- you've described how the -- you say the shelling started three days after you'd had a meeting in the field in Josava. Can you remember exactly when was it, the very end of March or the very beginning of April? Can you put a date on when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: It was sometime in early April, the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- and then in your original statement - but you've since corrected that, apparently - you said that the shelling lasted for five weeks. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Those five weeks referred to the entire period of time starting from the hand-over of weapons, the shelling, and their arrival in Blagaj. But the actual shelling lasted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Apparently -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. 044, the interpreters couldn't hear the last answer you gave. Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The actual shelling, the hand-over of weapons and the arrival in Blagaj Japra lasted for about six weeks, but the shelling, the actual shelling lasted one week only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying that this was just some slip or mistake in your original statement?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: It was not my mistake. It could have been a mistake in translation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's look at paragraph 17. It's the -- 1-7. It's the same numbering in your version as the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just ask, Your Honour, I'm afraid I'm not clear about this, whether the interpreters have the witness's statement in B/C/S in front of them. Do they have that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Otherwise, it seems a bit silly if I read the English statement, it gets translated into B/C/S, and the translation comes out slightly differently from the witness's statement. It's more sensible if they have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to ask them to translate it again or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's that -- well, they -- what I -- what I would invite them to do, if that's not inconvenient, is if I, if I have to, if I read out a sentence or so from the English translation of the witness's statement, it would be more convenient if the interpreters were then to adopt the witness's B/C/S statement as their translation. Otherwise, we get slightly different versions, which is -- it's confusing for the witness, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, and this is an excellent solution apart from the situation where the translation is not fully correct, because then your invitation would be to let the inconsistency between the B/C/S and the English version to continue to exist, because you invite them to give exactly the same translation as they find it in their B/C/S version, but if there's any mistake, this would be a mistake to -- to get an eternal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just trying to work out in my own head, Your Honour. If the statement was initially prepared in B/C/S then that problem doesn't arise because any errors in the translation will have been from B/C/S to English, so the problem, Your Honour, refers to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you start with the English text and you invite those -- our interpreters to take exactly the literal B/C/S text, then the same mistake would be made in the other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is any.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm still not following Your Honour, because what the interpreters are being invited to do will be effectively to read out as their translation what was the original statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we would have a wrong understanding of it. Therefore, that's the reason why I thought that where the witness has at least left it open that there might have been a mistake in translation or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. perhaps even in writing down, although we find his initials not under the original but only under the English version --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if -- yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If I can just correct the record a little. The statement is prepared during the interview with the witness in the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because it says that it's language used in interview is Bosnian and English, as the front page says. You say the interview was held in English and was then translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. The general practice is that statement would be written in English, read back to the witness by the interpreter on the spot in B/C/S and the written translation is prepared back here in The Hague in English. So the original written statement is in English and not in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's also the one that was signed, at least identified by the witness through his initials on the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, with all this knowledge in mind, Mr. Stewart, I'm certain that you'll find a proper course for consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe my logic was impeccable based on wrong statement, which was my assumption that the statement was originally prepared in B/C/S. We have approached that in a slightly crab-wise manner but we've got there in the end. So I'll just follow the simple course then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The paragraph 17, I'm reading from the English, of course: "The shelling lasted for five weeks. On the sixth week, the Serb soldiers came into the village and told us that we had to leave. During the last week they shelled us mostly at night." Now, what I'm suggesting to you, Witness, is that it's a pretty substantial correction to those three sentences to reduce the period of shelling from five weeks to one week, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: There was shooting throughout those five weeks, however, this one week as the worst, and that was the week when the shelling took place. However, as for the remainder of the time, those five weeks, they opened fire from surrounding hills, they shot in the air, and it is correct that they -- that there was shooting throughout those six weeks, however, what had to be emphasised here was that the actual shelling lasted for one week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there was in that six-week period, there was several weeks, were there, without shelling, followed, towards the end of that period, by one week of shelling. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the shelling came only in the last week or two of that six-week period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: That's right. After the hand-over of weapons. Before the weapons were handed over, there was only shooting, sporadic shooting, from small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think we'd better get the time scale clear now, then. The hand-over of weapons that you've described took place at the very end of March. That's correct on your evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: End of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. So let's go back to paragraph 12 of your statement, then, to clarify that. It starts off: "At the end of March 1992, there were some meetings set up with the Serbs and the SDA." And Mr. Barjaktarevic was called over to the village of Josava to meet the SDA president, and you say: "As a result of this meeting, the Muslims surrendered the weapons." And then you go on to describe the search that you mentioned from 11.00 to 4.00 p.m. Are you saying that the period covered by paragraph 12 of your statement from the initial meeting set up to the search for weapons that took place from 11.00 to 4.00 p.m., are you saying that that was a period of several weeks?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This was taking place over a period of several weeks. Sifet didn't attend only one meeting but several meetings. The last time he went and came back, he said that the best solution would be for us to hand over the weapons and that after that everything should be back to normal. Dzafer and Resad came to that meeting at Bosanski Novi, and they confirmed, they agreed that this would be the best solution, and that is when we organised the hand-over of weapons. We went to the village of Josava, to the field there, and it was after that that the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 18 of your statement, you say: "There was no organised defence in Bosanski Novi. We had no weapons." And that's been your evidence, that there were no weapons at all. So the -- however long the shelling took, it took place in relation to a village which had no defences at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any attempt during that week of shelling that you've described by any Serb forces to enter your village?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: They did not enter the village directly. However, after the shelling, they remained on the surrounding hills. We could see them. But they did not come to the village itself apart from the two soldiers in a Pinzgauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you described the organisation of a convoy of approximately 8.000 people. Who organised that?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No one in particular. Serb soldiers created panic amongst the people, and in Donji -- Gornji Agici, they directed the population in the direction of Prijedor. Then they set the local petrol station on fire, as well as some houses, and then we headed toward Bosanski Novi because we realised that was the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a specific event or a specific change of the pattern of what are broadly called military activity which triggered off that organisation of a convoy?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes. When the two soldiers arrived in a Pinzgauer, they looked for Sifet Barjaktarevic and they said that we had to leave our houses because allegedly they were no longer able to protect us or defend us.
