From whom, I don't know. They said that there were paramilitary formations in the area, that they could not control them, that they had slipped out of control. This is what we were told by the Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 20 of your statement, you refer to -- you've made an amendment to your statement since it was originally given so that the sentence which began: "They took two men out of the crowd," now reads that: "A group of Serbian military police separated two brothers," and you gave their names, Nijaz and Karanfil Isakovic, and bound their hands. You knew those brothers, did you?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I knew the brothers and I knew the soldiers from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You knew the soldiers by name, did you?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They had been civilians up until that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were they by any chance brothers, the two soldiers? Because you gave their names.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, they were children of two brothers. They were cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I see. And the -- do you know any reason why the Isakovic brothers would have been separated out at that point?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: In my opinion, they were rather well off. They wanted money from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So they obviously had known each other before. The two cousins and the two brothers, they had known each other; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the cousins, the Messrs. Grab, you refer to them as military policemen. What sort of policemen were they?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: They were military police officers wearing camouflage uniforms and flak jackets and they were standing on the road there. They were not members of the regular military police. They had just put on this attire when the eviction of the population started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 23 of your statement, you refer to the decision that you could stay in the village of Blagaj, this is after the organised convoy that you've described. You say: "The women and children were placed in houses and the men stayed and slept in garages and on tractors." How many men are you talking about there who stayed and slept in garages and on tractors?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: We were anywhere between 3 and 4.000 if you're referring to all men. But if you're referring only to military-aged men, then we were 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I'm referring to, so that we get it specific and there's no doubt, your sentence talks about women and children being placed in houses, and on the other hand the men, as opposed to the children, the men stayed and slept in garages and on tractors. And I'm asking you in that particular phrase in your statement, when you talk about the men who stayed and slept in garages and on tractors, how many of those men there were. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Sir, I'm really unable to give you the exact number, because first we were stopped in the village of Blagaj, and then we were put up in several houses. In the house where I slept, there were 52 of us. We did not want the women and children to sleep in the garages, so we put them in the houses and we slept in the garage. And I think this was the case with every house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I suggest to you, Witness, that you talk about the negotiations lasting for 17 days then when you were in this village, that you must have some rather better idea of how many men there were staying and sleeping in garages and on tractors in this village at that time, and I'm inviting you to give the Trial Chamber as good an idea as you can of the number.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: We were about 8.000, that is all of us, all the residents, together with the residents of Blagaj Japra, including women and children, and all able-bodied men slept out in the open so the women, children, and the elderly could have enough room in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is your answer that there was still something like 8.000 people being squeezed into the village of Blagaj in the way that you've described?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, but when I say "people," I include women, children, the elderly; all of us. As for the able-bodied men, there were 700 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it was the able-bodied men who were sleeping in garages and on tractors, was it?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. Children slept with women inside, as did the elderly and the sick. This was perfectly normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So to get it straight, there were 700 or so, you said, that you put in the category of able-bodied men from which it follows that there were over 7.000 people who were outside that category, either women, children, or men who were too old or in some other way not able-bodied; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I said this because I learned the exact number of able-bodied men in the camp once they drew up the list. That is, while we were on the train and after we had been separated by the Serb soldiers, there were 700 of us. There may have been more able-bodied men in Blagaj, I don't know, but in the camp we learned that there were 700 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's only this -- I'm sorry to keep picking away at this, but your description so far is that you have a convoy of about 8.000 people - it's my word, but they're obviously squeezed into the village of Blagaj because 8.000 is a lot of people for a village to accommodate - that more than seven-eighths of that convey consist of people who were not able-bodied men. Now, that's right so far? You agree with that as a correct summary of what you are saying to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Out of that 7 to 8.000 people, there may have been as many as 3.000 able-bodied men, but once we were put on the train and taken to Ostruzna, then a Serb soldier singled out 700 able-bodied men who were eventually thrown at the Bosanski Novi football stadium. In Blagaj, there may have been anywhere between 3 and 4.000 able-bodied men. I am talking only about the 700 that had been singled out by Serb soldiers in Ostruzna and sent to the football stadium in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would invite you, Witness, to concentrate very carefully on the questions because we had a little bit of understandable confusion, perhaps, about mosques earlier, but when I am asking you about the time in the village and I'm not asking you about the time in the camp, would you please do your very best to keep your answers to the area that I'm asking about because otherwise it becomes totally confusing. Would you please do that. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I do. While we were in Blagaj those 17 days, there were between 2.500 and 3.000 able-bodied men who slept in the garages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there were enough garages for them, and tractors, were there?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, there were. Including everything; stables, tractors, trailers. People slept on trailers, underneath the trailers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraph 25 -- and can we be clear what we're talking about: You have given evidence that after the 17 days of negotiation and the failure to reach agreement, the soldiers surrounded the village of Blagaj, and then you talk about the JNA soldiers attacking the civilian population. And then you say: "The shooting began and civilians were wounded." Was the shooting that you're mentioning there one-way in the sense that Serbs were shooting but nobody was shooting at them? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say in paragraph 25: "The shooting began and civilians were wounded," were any civilians killed on that occasion in that shooting?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, not that -- on that occasion. Only two civilians were wounded, but nobody got killed. They just wanted to create fear and panic. But once we crossed the bridge, they started killing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You refer in paragraph 30 to a man named Dragan who came in a Lada. Do you know his other name?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, I don't. I learnt that his name was Dragan only after he had left, because people who happened to be around me told me that this was Dragan from Svodna who had worked at the registry -- registrar's office before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Gaynor, is there any need for re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No need, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I should like to clarify a detail with you. In your statement, you make mention of the fact that you received food once per day, and on page 21 of the transcript, you said - and I will quote you in English - I would like to see if this is a clerical error, a typing error, or a slip of the tongue. How do you respond to that? Did you receive food once every day or once a week?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No. We received food once a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me now move to the incident involving the helicopter which you mentioned in your statement. You said - again I'll quote in English - paragraph 14: [In English] "I did see a military helicopter land in a nearby hamlet called Halilovici." [Interpretation] My question with respect to that is as follows: What were you doing at the moment when you noticed this helicopter land?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I happened to be outside in the yard of my house. As to what I was doing, nothing out of the ordinary. I was just outside my home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What time was it, approximately? Was it during the morning, during the day, in the evening?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at about what time in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: At about 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And you were able to identify a military helicopter as well as two vehicles?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were able to identify to see the drivers of these two vehicles? So where exactly did this helicopter land; in a field or ...

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The helicopter landed between two hills in the hamlet of Zablacka [phoen] near Halilovici. Ten minutes later, the two vehicles, which were civilian vehicles, arrived. One of them was a Lada, and the other one was a Warburg. I was not alone at that time. There were two other people with me, so we wanted to see what this was all about. Mostly we could observe aircraft over flying in the direction of Croatia, but this was the first time that a helicopter landed. And as we were going towards the helicopter, these two vehicles overtook us carrying weapons, and before we were able to reach the spot where the helicopter was, it took off again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, you went there to see what was happening. You left your home, and you headed out in the direction of the spot where the helicopter had landed. You and several other people, your friends.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How far were you from the helicopter? How long did it take for the helicopter to land? Actually, how long did it remain grounded?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: For about 20 to 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the distance between the spot where you were and the place where the helicopter had landed was how many metres or kilometres?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Maybe one kilometre as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were walking towards the helicopter, to the spot where it had landed. However, you did not manage to cover all of this distance, because in the meantime the helicopter left that spot. It was no longer there. And you saw two vehicles coming back or going where? In what direction were these two vehicles moving?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see these two vehicles. They were coming back from the spot where the helicopter was, in the direction of the village of Josava. As we were moving towards the helicopter, they were already on their way back, and the helicopter had taken off in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was then that you were able to identify the two drivers?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it was these two drivers who took it upon themselves to unload the weapons, to place them into the two vehicles, or were there others, other people helping them?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anybody else, just the two drivers in the car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you as well. My first question is you mentioned Ostruzna as the place where the able-bodied men separated from the women, children, and elderly in the train; correct?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with place called Stanari?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I have heard of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know where that is, and do you know where it is in relation to Ostruzna?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I think it's between Prijedor and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In your statement, you said that the range of these weapons, and you were then referring to 60- and 80-millimetre mortars, are -- the range of these weapons are 1.200 metres.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I did -- that's what I said. Roughly. I can't give you any exact figures. But yes, it was approximately 1.200 metres. That was the range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you mean to say that this was the range that they were shooting from or more in general terms, that the maximum range of 60- and/or 80-millimetre mortars is 1.200 metres?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I meant to say that that was the maximum range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Maximum range, 1.200 metres. You said that the shelling was coming from two Serb villages, Josava and Krslje. What is the distance of those two villages from where you were?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: As the crow flies in a straight line, about one kilometre, thereabouts. 800 metres perhaps. Anyway, across the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you have any specific knowledge about mortars or did you want to express that the range was sufficient to cover the distance from where they were shooting from to the place where you were, or do you have any further specific knowledge of mortars and ranges of mortars?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I don't know anything much about mortars, but I do know the direction that the shells come from. When a shell explodes or, rather, after the explosion, you can find the make the shell and its origin. So the direction it comes from is where you'll find this fragment lodged in the soil, in the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My last question also refers to the helicopter incident. Did you discuss with other people your observations as far as blankets and weapons hidden under a blanket are concerned? Did you discuss that with others?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, when we returned, when we went back. We gathered together in front of a shop, a centre there, and we were wondering what they were doing, what was going on, what was happening, and that's all. Later on, of course, we learnt what it was all about and what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you think about weapons at that moment being transported under a blanket?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: When I saw weapons being transported under a blanket, I realised that they were arming the Serb population from the surrounding villages and that the time would come for us to move out, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you the driver of the car you were in when you saw this other car driving in the opposition direction where you observed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. weapons under a blanket? Were you driving your own car or were you a passenger in that car?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No, no, I was on foot. I was walking, and the vehicles were driven by two Serbs, and they approached me. I was walking along. I didn't have a car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for these answers. Does the -- have the questions by the Bench raised any need for further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they have, very briefly. It's Your Honour's questions in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness can have -- I hope this is a convenient request. I'm looking at a map of Bosanski Novi municipality which was in the batch of material provided to us. It's got the reference number 0402-2625, Bosanski Novi Municipality. Is that something which can be brought up on the screen for the witness to see?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it been used in evidence before?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I believe it hasn't this morning. I think we used a different map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have to look to Ms. Annink.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was looking, Your Honour, as well, in effect, to Ms. Annink-Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks, Ms. Annink-Javier, as if it appears on the list of potential exhibits under 39.084. At least, there I find this same number. Is it possible to have this on the screen? In the description it's called Bosanski Novi map number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could deal with this more quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could put it on the ELMO, perhaps, and in the meantime Ms. Annink-Javier can -- and could it be shown for one second to Mr. Gaynor so that he at least knows what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's not a very complex point, Your Honour, so really we'll manage pretty well with a piece of paper, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've got it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In answer to His Honour Judge Orie's questions, Witness, about the distance of the villages of Josava and Krslje from your village, Suhaca, you said, I think, that each village was one kilometre away as the crow or the helicopter flies. That's right, isn't it? That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have a look at the map so far as you need to, but the position is quite clear, isn't it, that Josava is quite obviously two kilometres away and not one, and Krslje is quite obviously five kilometres away from Suhaca, isn't it, and not one?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, but not in a straight line, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Witness: As the crow flies, you can draw a line quite clearly, because that's all you do on a map, just a straight line from Suhaca to each of those villages, and there's a scale on that piece of paper as well. It's absolutely clear, isn't it, that Josava is two kilometres away from Suhaca and Krslje is five kilometres away. As near as makes no significant difference at all.

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Well, if you want more exact data, then the point from the village of Josava is not in the right place. It would be more towards -- to the left, towards Suhaca in fact. Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're saying the map's wrong or that your evidence when you're talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before continuing, Mr. Stewart, could I have the exact location, because it's not in my mind that I asked for distances between villages, but I think I asked for the distance between where the witness was, which is, of course, not the same as -- let me just -- and I'd like to have it a bit more zoomed in because I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's available in colour now if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Then perhaps we move to the computer evidence and see whether we have a more clear picture. And perhaps we zoom in at the relevant part. I do understand. Let's just -- could you take this out for a second, because it seems that there was a -- yes. The problem is the bottom line, where there's information which should not be there. This video will be -- this video part will be -- this computer evidence part will be redacted to the extent that that part of the picture will be taken out. Could you create a picture without the -- yes. You've got it now? Then we could again move to the computer evidence where we now have no toolbar any more on the bottom. At least, I hope. I don't see anything at all at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this will take a moment or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'll trial to make progress, Your Honour, while we're waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where you were -- what His Honour says is of course absolutely correct. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I have my piece of paper back, actually, if we're going to be operating from the screen. I wonder if I could have the paper back which I handed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My problem with the paper was that I couldn't read it on my screen, Mr. Stewart. So I was only too happy to have a technically sophisticated picture on my screen, but then we have other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have a similar problem, Your Honour, when this screen is on, so it happens to us all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Witness, I think perhaps the most -- the best thing would be to establish where you were, because His Honour did ask you how far -- I acknowledge that entirely -- how far the villages of Josava and Krslje were from where you were, and where do you say you were?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I was in the village of Suhaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said -- I think, a few minutes ago you suggested that your location hadn't been pinpointed sufficiently accurately, and I think you were suggesting there was a difference between the position of Suhaca marked on the map and where you actually were. Is that what you're saying or not?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No. The point on the map is exact, and that's where I was, where Suhaca was. But you wanted more exact information as to the kilometres between and the distance between Josava and Krslje. And if you look at the point where Suhaca is to be found and where Josava is to be found, then the Josava point should be a little more towards the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not following. Are you saying the map is wrong?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: For such precise data, the kind that you're asking about, no, it is not accurate enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps zoom in on the relevant part of the map but including the kilometre scale as we find just under the legend, because that would -- I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I caused a lot of problem, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I comment this. This is, in effect, potentially a time saving and it isn't really my giving evidence. It is a simple fact that if one measures the distance between these villages against the scale on the map, that the village of Josava is, on the map, 2 kilometres from Suhaca. It just is. And the village of Krslje is five kilometres from Suhaca. According to the map, it simply is, and no elaboration with the witness poring over the map is going to change that simple fact. So actually what I'm seeking from the witness is really very simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, I'm inviting you to acknowledge that your evidence that each village was one kilometre from where you were - in fact you said even perhaps 800 metres - your evidence earlier that it was one kilometre is not just wrong, but for somebody with local knowledge, as you have, was simply obviously not true. Do you acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: I agree because villages have houses, and they are set apart, but the Serbs, the soldiers who shot at us, shot at us from the surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's not the question you were asked. And what I'm suggesting to you is that you came here, took the solemn declaration, you've got here to tell the Trial Chamber, and you have been in this particular respect apart from anything else, you have been quite exceptionally casual and careless in the evidence that you've given to this Trial Chamber. Do you now acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: No. I said how it was and I told the truth. These small discrepancies are just -- well, you asked where they shot at from those mortars, or did you ask where the houses making up the village of Josava lie and where they were?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: The president of this particular Trial Chamber asked you very specifically how far these villages were from where you were. Let's take Krslje. You said one kilometre, perhaps 800 kilometres. Now, you lived there. Krslje is five kilometres away, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Krslje as a village is five kilometres away from Suhaca, but the gentleman asked me about the mortars and where they were shooting from and where they were shelling there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't need or wish to pursue this point any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do I formally need to tender the map, Your Honour? Ms. Cmeric suggests that -- the map we've just been looking at, there's some formality I need to go through to make sure it's in the right place for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be good to have, since specific reference is made to this scale on this map, that we have that in evidence. If you have not yet prepared copies, then that could be solved at a later moment, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We need it back if we are to prepare copies, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the next question is who is going to prepare the copies. The registrar, which means that you have got a lot of credit with her, will make the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any questions for the Prosecution in respect of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just one or two questions, Your Honour, in respect of his knowledge of military hardware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sir, is it right that you completed mandatory military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: How long was that military service?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: One year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you observe JNA helicopters during your service?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Well, that's quite usual throughout my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you also observe AK-47s and other kinds of rifles?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did come across different weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And did you observe shells, shell casings?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, shells; 60 millimetres, 80 millimetres, the Scorpio type of pistol, the automatic TM rifles, machine-guns, hand-held mortars, Howitzers, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And during the period of your military service, did you have frequent occasion to deal with weapons and to observe helicopters?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, I did. While I was doing my military service, I was the charger, the gunner on a recoilless rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And your military service was about two years prior to these events; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness 044.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. 1989, June, was when I joined the army, or rather, when I went to the army, and I returned in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gaynor. Witness O44, or should I say 044, it's not quite clear to me, but you've answered all the questions put to you by the parties and put to you by the Bench. I thank you very much for coming the long distance to The Hague, and it's important for this Tribunal to hear the testimony of those who were present at the time of the events persons are charged with. I'd like to wish you a safe trip home again. You're excused. Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that exhibit would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D11 has been written already on it by Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I formally request that the exhibits which we tendered be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The usual way of doing it is that now Madam Registrar will briefly describe all the exhibits tendered so that we have a full overview. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a comment about the statement, and it's a general comment. It won't help in relation to the very large number of statements that have already been prepared out in Bosnia and Republika Srpska, but it might just possibly help for the future, and we're not in the business, on the Defence side, of gratuitously criticising other people's work, but we are finding quite commonly, and we found in relation to that statement, that the chronology of events is perhaps not very specifically followed through when statements are taken, and that actually does create extra work, and it does take time in the course of cross-examination to sort out things which really would be more conveniently sorted out at the point when the statement is taken and prepared. So to the extent to which statements are being taken in future or there is any reasonable opportunity to correct or tidy them up, we would suggest that that would be a time saving for the Trial Chamber and all else -- everybody else concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As you may have noticed in respect of paragraph 17 of the statement, I immediately asked myself if five week was one week what the sixth week would be. So if you speak with witnesses, perhaps it would be good, if there's any change in the chronology or if there is any point where the chronology could be clarified, that the Prosecution tries to do that in advance so that we have as clear as possible chronology in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My only other observation is a very brief one, Your Honour. I mentioned this morning that we had had 89(F) statement only this morning. I don't want to suggest that is -- that is a big problem. It isn't. I've spoken to the Prosecution. It's only -- I say only, it's important for its purpose that the public should know but it is a summary of existing material. I had indicated that provided we receive these summaries by, say, 9.00 p.m. the night before by e-mail, then owing to the slightly different working habits of the members of the Defence team, that would ensure that we were able to pick them up in good time and have time to have a read through, because of course we know that they are just summaries and the Prosecution will be preparing them in a professional way anyway, so they don't require huge input of work, and that would be entirely satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have seen that I -- you may have heard that the Chamber supports your slight criticism on matters delivered at breakfast rather than the day before, and I would say 9.00 p.m. is rather generous.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Also, the transcript rather suggests that the Prosecution brought my breakfast to me. I have made that request, but so far I can't persuade either the Prosecution or my Defence team to provide that service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes you get newspapers with breakfast, sometimes you get other documents. Let's continue. Madam Registrar, Mr. Stewart interrupted you when you started -- wanted to start to read the list of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P93 under seal, the pseudonym sheet. Exhibit P94, photograph of destroyed mosque in Suhaca. Exhibit P95, record of exhumation dated 28 October 1998. And P95.1, the English translation. P96, report for the Bosanski Novi public security station dated 15 August 1992. And P96.1, the English translation. P97, under seal, witness -- witness statement dated 11 December 1998, and addendum dated 1st of June, 2001. And P97.1, the B/C/S translation. D11, a map of Bosanski Novi municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since there are no objections, all these exhibits are admitted into evidence, where applicable under seal. Before we ask the Prosecution to call its next witness, let's just first verify there are no protective measures in force, as far as I understand, and I do understand that it will be Mr. Karabeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, I was informed that you would cross-examine Mr. Karabeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes. And I also understood as an initiative welcomed by the Chamber that you would like to, I would say, replace part of the cross-examination by tendering cross-examination -- transcripts of cross-examination in other cases; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. What I propose to do is in fact tender the cross-examination already performed in the Brdjanin trial in respect of both the next witnesses that I will be cross-examining, that is, Mr. Begic and Mr. Karabeg, and that will in effect leave very little cross-examination for Mr. Begic and a much more streamlined cross-examination for Mr. Karabeg. And there is no protective measures for either of the two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but there is one issue that is the public character of this trial. That is point one. Does that mean that where we -- when we I would say introduce short versions of whether these are statements under 89(F) or whether this is our transcripts, we usually have a summary. Did you prepare also a summary for those elements of cross-examination so that the public knows what has been said and --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's concern, of course, but what I propose to do is, in my cross-examination, briefly highlight the high points of that previous cross-examination. I thought that was the best way of ensuring the public character as well as saving time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that also mean that by highlighting you also give some guidance to the Chamber what are the most relevant parts of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no idea how many pages there are, but the Chamber is a bit hesitant to -- we've seen some testimonies of over a thousand pages, but that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It's nothing like that. I'm just going to consult with my fellow counsel for a second. [Defence counsel confer] .

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, if I may, I'm just reminded by my fellow counsel that if I give the page references and what have you, it's all on the Internet in any event, and the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree there is a difference between a statement which is not yet public. On the other hand, there's another issue. I take it that if you use the transcript, is that 89(F) then, in your view, or would it be 92 bis -- 92 bis under (D)?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: That's actually a very good question, Your Honour, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Because I did give that some thought over the weekend as to in which particular category it might fall, and it's an interesting point. The answer, Your Honour, is that I still think it's rather a moot point, but seeing the witness is here, then it could be said to be 89(F). In view of the strictures in relation to ensuring that where one contemplates 92 bis (D) transcript that the procedures of 92 bis should be followed, there's also an argument that it's 92 bis (D). And when one looks further at some of the comments that were made in that interlocutory appeal in Milosevic in relation to the use of 89(F) and 92 bis (D), it is an interesting point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- the Prosecution is invited to, not necessarily at this very moment, but to give it some thought. It might be relevant for the Prosecution sooner or later as well, especially if it ever comes to presentation of the Defence case, and when introducing transcripts of witnesses given in other cases. Well, I take it that the parties do agree that either 92 bis (D) or under 89(F) we can proceed this way. Let's then do it and if there are any further observations to be made, the Chamber is quite willing to hear them. Not at this moment necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly. It's our preliminary view that 92 bis (D) is lex specialis in respect of transcripts, and if a party seeks admission of a transcript of evidence, it does so pursuant to 92 bis (D). Now, 92 bis gives the other party two weeks in which to respond to an application under Rule 92 bis. Now, while we certainly won't seek to hold up the proceedings today in respect of that time limit, we do reserve our position -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that it's not a view of the Prosecution that 92 bis (A) is lex specialis in respect of 89(F)?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, it's not our view, Your Honour, because when the witness is on the stand and able to attest to the veracity of the written statement, I think the Milosevic decision on 89(F) provides that the other requirements of 92 bis are not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's not -- let's not deal with it in its entirety, but it's the first time that the Defence has introduced, I think, transcripts as a way of introducing written evidence rather than oral evidence in cross-examination. That's just a point I wanted to -- I wanted to raise and to see whether there is any further observations to be made.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just one further observation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- just in relation to what was indicated from Mr. Gaynor in relation to the matter I raised about the Milosevic interlocutory appeal and then, of course, the further comments that were made about lex specialis. The distinction that Mr. Gaynor makes about the fact that 92 bis (A) is different from 92 bis (D) because in respect of the statement situation the witness is in the box, the same applies for the witness being in the box in respect of the transcript. You gave transcript on a previous occasion, you confirmed that you -- the evidence you gave on a prior occasion was the truth. It falls -- actually falls into the same category, I would submit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I don't know whether I fully agree but perhaps the Chamber should consider it in its entirety. Let's move, then, now forward. The next witness the Prosecution calls is Mr. Karabeg, if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I inquire at what time we were going to take the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next break will be in approximately 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I presume Mr. Karabeg. Mr. Karabeg, before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration is now being handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Mr. Hannis, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm prepared to hand this over. I meant to do it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I could hand the usher something to hand to the registrar. It's a list of the exhibits I propose to show this witness and the order in which I intend to show him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon. Would you tell us your name and spell it, please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Karabeg, K-a-r-a-b-e-g, and my first name is Mirzet, M-i-r-z-e-t.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would first like to show this witness copies of two ICTY statements that he's made. We have both English and B/C/S versions of his first statement dated 24 and 25 July 1999, and then a supplement dated 23 May 2002, making corrections to the first statement. And they are stapled together. I propose to treat them as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P98.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I would ask you to take a look at that statement, or actually those two statements, and tell us if you recognise those as statements you've previously made and that you've had a chance to review before today.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: These are my statements, the statements that I gave on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second statement, dated 23 May of 2002, was a statement in which you made a number of changes or corrections to your first statement in 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And yesterday, in preparing for your testimony today, did you have an occasion to go over these statements with me?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the course of doing that, sir, I think we found one additional paragraph where you noted that there should be made a change, and I would direct you to paragraph 88 in the July 1999 statement. And I'm reading the English, which says: "I was singled out with 14 others for beatings." And in counting the names of the persons there, I believe we found out that there were 11 names, and you indicated to me that that was incorrect. Either the translation was incorrect or it was written down incorrectly in that you were not singled out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Rather, these were the names of people you remembered who were beaten but not especially singled out?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No. No. See, when I told you yesterday about this, it involved an incident when all of us were beaten and not that a group had been singled out specifically for beating. This group, we were together at Betonirka. Most of us were in prison, and the majority of us, on the 28th of August, 1992, were sent to Manjaca. So we were amongst the last people to be sent to Manjaca. It was not a group that had been singled out for beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, with that one additional change, are you satisfied and can you confirm to the Court today that your written statements are true and correct and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, pursuant to Rule 89(F), we would like to offer those two statements as part of this witness's evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the summary, you'd start with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I intend to now read a brief summary of what is in his written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this provided before or after breakfast to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: This is the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was provided, in fact, after breakfast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Any problems with the summary as far as we know?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I in fact received it as I walked into court this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, timing of delivering of summaries has been discussed already. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Karabeg, I'm just now going to read a summary, and when I finish this I will have some additional questions for you. Your Honour, this witness is a Bosnian Muslim, a Bosniak born in Sanski Most, trained as a lawyer, and worked in the Famos metal manufacturing factory as chief of personnel. He was an SDA candidate during the 1990 multi-party elections, and he became president of the Executive Board of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly, holding that position from 1 January 1991 until 17 April 1992. He describes the election results and the make-up of the Municipal Assembly, noting Nedeljko Rasula, a Serb and SDS member, became president of the Municipal Assembly. He names other leading figures in the local SDS. Also notes that the local JNA unit in early 1992 was the 6th Krajina Brigade under Colonel Branko Basara. The witness states that the SDS Serbs began insisting on dividing the municipality along ethnic lines and creating a separate Serbian municipality of Sanski Most which would align itself with the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina, ARK. A first step in the process was the 11 April 1992 reorganisation of the police force with new insignia and a loyalty oath to the Republika Srpska, RS. The SDS Serbs continued to insist on a division of the municipality and wanted the non-Serbs to move to the other side of the river. Many checkpoints were set up in the municipality and all non-Serbs would be stopped and searched. On 17 April 1992, the SDS Serbs and the SDA and HDZ representatives continued to negotiate the situation. The SDS representatives said that they could not control their extremists and that the non-Serbs had to leave the municipal building right away. This witness and other non-Serbs, including about 36 non-Serb policemen, went to the municipal building and took position there. Negotiations continued for a couple of days with the SDS Serbs showing a map proposing a street-by-street division of Sanski Most into two separate municipalities. On 19 April, Rasula gave an ultimatum to the non-Serbs in the municipal building that if they did not leave by 2200 hours and surrender all arms, they would be attacked. The non-Serbs noticed a column of about 30 vehicles of the 6th Krajina Brigade approaching and decided to quickly depart from the building to Sehovic. Serbs did attack the building. On 20 April the two sides met together with JNA General Momir Talic. The non-Serbs made several requests which were approved by Talic. The local SDS Serbs did not comply with the approved request. Local Serbs were part of an armed paramilitary group called the Serbian Liberation Force, SOS, which the witness believes was responsible for a series of shootings and bombings directed against the property of non-Serbs in early 1992 in Sanski Most. After 20 April 1992, JNA Colonel Basara had a series of meetings in the town and surrounding villages, promising to keep the peace and to deal with extremists in the SDS and SOS. The non-Serbs asked him to re-establish contact with the Serb leaders of Sanski Most, but he never did. The witness describes his arrest on 25 May 1992 and subsequent detentions at the Sanski Most prison, at Betonirka camp, and eventually at Manjaca. He talks about the terrible conditions and the constant beatings, including ones in which he lost all his teeth. On one occasion he was told that the beating was done based on the order of the chief of police Mirko Vrucinic. The witness never received any medical care while he was detained. Your Honour, that completes my reading of the summary. Perhaps now would be a good time for our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we best could have the break now. Mr. Karabeg, questions will be put to you, but not until after the break. We'll have a break until ten minutes to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I understand from your statement that you became the President of the Executive Board for Sanski Most municipality in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Just a slight correction; not Bosanski Novi but Sanski Most, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies; I was thinking of the last witness. And, sir, would you explain to the Judges, please, a little bit about how the municipal government in Sanski Most worked. First of all, explain to us about the Municipal Assembly. How was that made up and what was their responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is how it was: The elections were held in 1990, and following the electoral results in the Sanski Most municipality, if we look at the parties, the SDS won the majority vote, and therefore it had 23 seats in the Municipal Assembly. The SDA won 22 seats in the Municipal Assembly, and the HDZ won four seats, and the leftist forces 11. On the basis of these election results, a proposal was put forward by which the election results were to be put into practice. As the SDS received the largest number of votes and had 23 seats, they had the right to chose whether they wished to put forward a president of the Assembly or president of the Executive Board. They opted for the president of the Municipal Assembly, and there was secret ballot on the part of 60 members as to the nominations. So the Assembly was led by the president of the Assembly, the deputy Municipal Assembly president, and that was the representative of the HDZ party, Anto Tunjic, and president of the Executive Board. They were nominated and the elections were put into practice as president of the Assembly, as nominated, Rasula Nedeljko, was elected, I was the president -- as the SDA president, I became president of the Executive Board, and Anto Tunjic for the Municipal Assembly president. So within that context after the elections, the proposals were that the executive authority be elected with the Executive Board at its head, and I was the head of the Executive Board. Now, to the Executive Board we had three representatives to make it up, Bosniaks, Muslims, and then three representatives of the SDS party of Serb ethnicity and one representative of the Croatian ethnicity. So that was the composition of the Executive Board. It numbered seven members, of which three were Bosniaks, three were Serbs, and one was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may stop you there, Mr. Karabeg. Can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the relationship was between the Executive Board and the Municipal Assembly. How were laws made in Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is how it was: The laws and regulations were passed at the Assembly. That's where the decisions were taken, conclusions made, and other acts passed, like the statute, the rules and regulations, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did the Executive Board --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the Executive Board did with regard to laws that were passed by the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The Executive Board would implement those laws, and as it is called the Executive Board, the Executive Board executes. It was the executive power, and the Assembly was the legislative power.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many votes did it take for the Executive Board to agree --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did it take a unanimous decision by the Executive Board or merely a majority of the seven to reach agreement on a decision?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is how it was: We had our rules governing our work, the way in which matters were voted on. So everything was regulated by law through these rules, and decisions were made by a two-thirds majority. And the work of the Executive Board could start if the Executive Board meetings were attended by more than half the members, but decisions were always taken by majority vote, a simple majority vote with the total number of members present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us how the -- how the paperwork was processed. Once a decision was passed, a new statute, a new regulation, a new decision, how was that put into effect? Who needed to sign it? Did it need any kind of seal or stamp, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It was signed and stamped by the president of the Assembly, and the power was vested in him. That was law. Decisions and conclusions were passed by the Assembly, and they were signed by the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was there any official seal required to make that law take valid effect?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is how it was: For a signature to be valid and for procedure to be put into effect, a seal was, of course, necessary, yes. The signature had to be accompanied with a seal for it to be further implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the seal go on every copy of an order or were there other copies that did not require a seal?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is how it was: Every particular -- in every particular case, how it should be dealt with was prescribed. The case in point, whether it was necessary for further work, of course a decision would be made, signed, and sealed, a stamp placed on it. Now, depending on how much time had elapsed for the document to be implemented, and if that time had the -- the deadline had passed by for its implementation, it was filed in the archives, and then you would sometimes have signatures on that without a seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I want to ask you about a couple of other members of the local SDS party. Did you know a Vlado Vrkes?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was he and what was his position in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Vlado Vrkes was the president of the SDS party in Sanski Most or, rather, the president of the municipal board of the SDS Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a Boro Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Boro Savanovic was a member of the leadership of the SDS. I think it was the same as the Executive Board in their party. The municipal Executive Board of the SDS, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to refer your attention to March of 1991. In your position as president of the Executive Board for Sanski Most, did you have occasion to attend a conference in Banja Luka around that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and this is what happened: On my table, I found an invitation that a meeting be organised in Banja Luka. Nobody handed it to me, I just happened to find it on my table one morning. And the next day I went to Banja Luka. I assumed that it was -- it had been placed on my table because the president of the Assembly, Nedeljko Rasula, was not in Sanski Most on that particular day. Anyway, I went to the conference hall of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, and when I got there, I found a lot of people there. I did not know them, but I met the president of the Executive Board of the Kljuc municipality, Asim Egeric, and I asked him, "How come you're here? It seems that we have wandered into this meeting." And he said, "I don't know. I found an invitation, and I responded to the invitation." So that's how I came to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what kind of meeting was this and how many people were attending?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, there might have been up to a hundred people there, and later on I realised that they were the presidents of the municipal assemblies and boards and party presidents, and some other people there. I really can't say who they all were, but anyway, they were from the municipalities of the Bosanska Krajina region, as it was called at the time. So they were representatives, that is to say the leaders of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the president of -- I believe it was the Executive Board in Kljuc. Was he also a Serb?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Asim Egeric was a Bosniak, a Muslim. May I just be allowed to say something at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Three days later I found this all a bit suspicious because on the territory of those 17 municipalities of Bosanska Krajina, there was only one Bosniak who was president of the municipality, and he was Muhamed Cehajic. That was his name. Three days later, when I happened to be in Prijedor, I asked him, I said, "Muhamed, tell me, please, did you receive an invitation to attend that meeting in Banja Luka?" And he said, "I didn't receive any invitation." And he was surprised that the meeting had taken place. So that's why I think it was only the representatives of the Serb people who were invited to attend that particular meeting. So as the chief of the head of the municipality, he ought to have been invited if all the other municipality presidents from the Bosanska Krajina region, the 17 municipalities, had been invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you and Mr. Egeric the only non-Serbs at this meeting, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That's right, we were. We were the only ones, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what do you recall about the topic that was discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: It was mentioned for the first time that Bosanska Krajina should be cleansed of the non-Serb people, that is to say that the media should be stifled first, the Croatian media or, rather, the Ustasha media, as they were referred to. And the Muslims were referred to as the balijas. So the Zagreb and Sarajevo media, in fact. And that at all cost the Serb people should be given the possibility of living in the area. And I remember very well when Judge Srbac [as interpreted], a judge of the misdemeanour court, said that the resources obtained from the penalties and taxes accrued would be siphoned off to this fund which would finance the functioning of Serbian media and Serbian television and that the Ustasha and balija medias or, rather, the Sarajevo and Zagreb media, and I mean television here, should be marginalised as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who any of the speakers were that talked about cleansing the Krajina of non-Serb people?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: I did not give much thought to the meeting at the time, and we were just present physically, if I could put it that way. Our presence was required, our physical presence, but we did think that the worst might come. So we did stay to the end of the meeting, but we tried to get away as soon as possible. So that was -- is what sticks out in my mind and what I remember best. And of course 14 years have gone by since then, so one doesn't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just before Mr. Hannis goes on, I'd just like to pick Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of these transcript matters as they occur. At line 16, page 82, line 16, there's a reference to, "And I remember very well when Judge Srbac..." In fact, that's not the name of the Judge. It's a reference to a Judge from a particular area called Srbac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from the place called Srbac. I don't remember the Judge's name. He was president of the misdemeanour court from Srbac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's been clarified. Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, I would like now if we could give the next item an exhibit number. It's a map with ERN 02296710. Mr. Karabeg, I'd like you to look at this map and we'll talk about the Krajina for a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P99.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, that's a map that shows Bosnia-Herzegovina with a portion of it coloured in red which was an area that later became known as the Autonomous Region of the Krajina. You mentioned at this March 1991 meeting, I think you referred to 17 municipalities. At that time, can -- or at this time can you recall which 17 municipalities were represented at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: It's like this: Those 17 municipalities which belonged to the Bosnian Krajina, I could tell you which they were on the basis of this map, and I would tell you the ones that didn't belong. For example, Bihac was never there, didn't belong to that, nor did Krupa, nor Petrovac, nor Drvar, for example. So these would be the rest of the municipalities belonging to the Bosnian Krajina because the others belonged to the Bihac region.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: And of course, the White Zazine and Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the Court, could you explain what the Bihac region was.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The Bihac region was as follows: Zazine, Velika Kladusa, Bihac, Bosanska Krupa, Bosanski Petrovac, Drvar, and Bosanski Novi. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can take that away now and I would like to show --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just be allowed to add that they were the districts on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If the next map could be given the next exhibit number and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P100.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, can you tell us what is on the screen in front of you now, or the ELMO to your right side.

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: On the screen we see the map of the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And does that accurately represent the geographic location of Sanski Most, the neighbouring municipalities, and most of the larger area --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, it does. It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And most --

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: The neighbouring municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And most of the larger villages within Sanski Most municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: That's right. Yes. In fact, these are the local communes of the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, or tell the Court a little bit about the ethnic make-up of Sanski Most municipality. How were the peoples divided among the three largest ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is how it was according to the 1991 population census: Sanski Most had 60.280 inhabitants, of which there were - and this might not be an exact figure, I might be wrong - but there were 28.300 Bosniaks, there were 25.000 Serbs or thereabouts, and there were about 4.280 Croats, and the others came under the rest or miscellaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could take that away and I would like to show him the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more map, Mr. Karabeg, relating to the ethnic distribution within Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P101.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, this is a map based on the 1991 census and showing in three different colours the distribution of the ethnic groups within Sanski Most municipality, with green for the Muslims or Bosniaks, blue for the Serbs, and red for the Croats. Based on your knowledge as a long-time resident of Sanski Most and president of the Executive Board, does this accurately depict the distribution of the various ethnic groups within those geographic locations in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: I think it does, yes. I think it does represent that. This is red, yes, that's right. This is the Croatian population. Yes, that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And within the town of Sanski Most itself, what was the ethnic distribution?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: This is how it was: I think that in Sanski Most the ratio was 45 per cent Muslims, Bosniaks, 45 per cent of them. The Serbs amounted to 10 per cent, 10 per cent Croats, and the rest were Serbs [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm done with that map, sir, and I would like to ask you to direct your attention to the summer of 1991. Do you recall a series of explosions and/or shootings directed against non-Serb businesses and properties in Sanski Most starting around that time?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Well, it started in April or May, I would say, 1991, when the explosions started, mostly in the various cafes whose proprietors were non-Serbs. And then this also -- this took place over two or three months. But as the 25th of May grew close, it became more frequent. So in May there would be two or three explosions, for example. And in other places there were 27. Now, these explosions -- well, one of the points on our agenda for the Executive Board meeting was this, that the investigation organs should uncover the perpetrators and that they be held accountable and brought to trial. But of course nothing was ever done. None of these perpetrators were ever uncovered. So the people who did this were never found.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me clear up something in your answer that I'm not sure of. You indicated that you think it began in April or May of 1991, and then you talked about it increasing, and as the 25th of May grew close, it became more frequent. Are you talking about the 25th of May, 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the 25th of May, 1992. I said that it had started either in May or in April. I think that the first explosion took place in April or in May, the next one in September, but as May grew closer, the explosions became more frequent. When the date of the 25th of May, as it was approaching in 1992, of course, they -- the explosions became more frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you have any idea what the approximate total number of explosions, these incidents in Sanski Most between the first one in spring 1991 on May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Twenty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in each case was the -- the victim business or premises a non-Serb property?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that particular point, I think that's a matter that the Prosecution should not lead on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, would it be better for you to reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, can you tell us as to those 27 incidents, whose property was the subject of the bombing in each of those 27 cases, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: In most of the cases Bosniaks, Muslims, and to a lesser extent Croats, for the simple reason that there were not that many Croat nationals in Sanski Most. So non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about an incident that you -- you wrote about, I think, in a document for the Executive Board in February of 1992. Do you recall an incident with regard to the -- the SDK, the public accounting service?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that incident. We, the parties, had divided the offices amongst ourselves, but as the events unfolded and as the situation changed -- for instance, in 1991, the SDS didn't much care about the SDK, however, at one point the SDK became interesting for them, and they requested that it be allocated to them. They were not successful in that request, however, and then through their prominent or extremist members, as they referred to them, they attempted a break-in into the SDK. They attempted to replace the man, the leader, the chief of the SDK by force, which was very interesting in the sense that the man in charge would then be able to send the funds in Banja Luka and not to Sarajevo as it was provided by law. I remember a lady by the name of Ankica who was a Croat and who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to stop for a second. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I notice that Mr. Karabeg has in front of him a document that he's reading from. In the circumstances where the document is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. No, no. You can take this away. These are just some copies that I have, but you're free to take this away. I don't need -- I don't need any of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's just appropriate that the document is moved to the side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The fact is that Mr. Karabeg had something in front of him, he said he's not reading from it. He doesn't need it. So let's continue. Please, Mr. Hannis, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think we did leave his statement in front of him because I anticipate referring to specific paragraphs in the future but I would ask him not read from it and if he does, to advise us when he's doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, Ms. Loukas cannot exactly see what is in front of you so she's entitled to find out whether, which has happened in the past, you would be reading or not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If she wants me to, I can give these to her. They are no secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has been clarified. There's no issue any more. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Karabeg, can you explain for us a little bit about what the SDK was in the municipalities in Bosnia in 1991 and 1992. What was that service? What was its function?

utterances.speaker: MIRZET KARABEG
utterances.text: In the territory of the former Yugoslavia, we had the so-called SDK, the public accounting service, through which all money transfers were made. So until that time, all of the funds were directed to the centre in Sarajevo, in accordance with the relevant provisions. We had SDKs at the level of the municipality, at the level of the republics, and at the level of the state, the state of the former Yugoslavia. So these funds included taxes, various types of dues and duties. I'm not sure of all the funds that went through the SDK. All of a sudden, the SDS wanted to have their men at the head of the SDK so that the funds could be redirected to Banja Luka.
